NUEVO LAREDO, Tamaulipas — Crews continue installing orange floating barriers in the Río Bravo between the two Laredos, and Mexico’s border water authority says the project has no permit on file — meaning it is moving forward outside the binational process established by the 1970 Boundary Treaty, according to El Mañana de Nuevo Laredo.

Ramón Meza González, representative of the Mexican Section of the International Boundary and Water Commission (CILA) in Nuevo Laredo, confirmed to the paper that his office has received no official documentation for the work now underway. The paper reports that segments have already been installed between the Colombia Bridge and International Bridge III, with recent expansion pushing the line of floats into residential neighborhoods including Siete Luces, Canta Ranas, La Ladrillera and Chacón.

The rollout began in early October, according to the report: airboats and heavy machinery entered the Texas side of the riverbank to drill into the riverbed and anchor steel fixtures, and by mid-month the first rotating buoys were set directly under the Juárez-Lincoln Bridge (Bridge II), sitting on exposed rock with the river at just 37 centimeters. The paper notes that a separate floating barrier episode in July, upstream near Eagle Pass and Piedras Negras, ended with more than 68 buoys torn loose by flooding and piled with debris against international bridge pilings — the scenario local officials say they fear repeating here.

Growing pushback

Last Saturday, dozens of Laredo residents, young people and environmental defenders marched the Las Palmas nature trail for Río Day, demanding the buoys stop and the border wall be cancelled, the paper reports. The demonstration included delivery of a citizen petition to U.S. Congressman Henry Cuellar. The mayors of both Laredos — Carmen Lilia Canturosas Villarreal of Nuevo Laredo and Dr. Víctor D. Treviño of Laredo — have also voiced opposition, with officials warning about safety risks and possible effects on COMAPA’s drinking-water intakes.

CILA says it is monitoring the situation while the infrastructure keeps advancing along the riverbed without international authorization.

Sources:

  • El Mañana de Nuevo Laredo: “Avanzan boyas pese a protestas; no tienen permiso de CILA” (Oct. 22, 2026)

Webb Watch 956
excerpt: Mexico's CILA says the orange floating barriers being installed in the Río Bravo between the two Laredos have no permit on file, bypassing the 1970 Boundary Treaty — even as the buoy line expands into residential neighborhoods and both mayors object.
title: River buoys advance between the two Laredos with no CILA permit, Mexico's water authority confirms
